name: Internal carotid artery
function: Paired source of the anterior cerebral circulation. After cervical and petrous segments, the ICA passes through the cavernous sinus, then enters the subarachnoid space as the supraclinoid segment. CN VI and sympathetic fibres lie beside the cavernous ICA; CN III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in the sinus lateral wall. Major distal branches are the ophthalmic, posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries, followed by the terminal ACA and MCA. These four segment names are a teaching simplification of more detailed segment classifications.

afferent: Common carotid artery at the carotid bifurcation
Possible collateral flow through the anterior or posterior communicating arteries; adequacy depends on individual anatomy and haemodynamics
efferent: Ophthalmic, posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries
Terminal ACA and MCA; lateral lenticulostriate arteries usually arise from M1, and the recurrent artery of Heubner usually arises near the ACA-ACoA junction or proximal A2, less often A1

bloodSupply: Inflow from the common carotid artery. Through its ACA, MCA, anterior choroidal and communicating branches it supplies variable cortical and deep territories; a fetal PCA configuration can extend the carotid territory into the occipital lobe.

clinical.findings: Clinical extent ranges from no deficit with effective collateral flow to retinal ischaemia, MCA-predominant infarction, watershed injury or a combined ACA/MCA infarction. Possible findings include contralateral weakness, sensory loss and homonymous field loss, with aphasia in a language-dominant hemisphere or neglect in the other hemisphere.
clinical.vascular: Internal carotid artery and its branches

clinical.findings: Transient monocular visual loss can result from ipsilateral carotid embolism or hypoperfusion of the retinal circulation; carotid disease is one of several possible causes.

clinical.syndrome: Cavernous ICA aneurysm or carotid-cavernous fistula
clinical.findings: Compression can affect ocular motor nerves and V1/V2 sensation. A fistula may cause proptosis, chemosis, pulsatile bruit and arterialized conjunctival veins. The cavernous ICA is extradural; haemorrhage patterns differ from intradural aneurysms.
May cause ipsilateral head or neck pain, partial Horner syndrome and cerebral or retinal ischaemia from thromboembolism or reduced flow.

name: Vertebral artery
synonyms: V1–V4 segments of the vertebral artery
function: Paired arteries arising from the subclavian arteries. V1 runs to the transverse foramen, V2 usually ascends through C6-C2 transverse foramina, V3 curves around the atlas, and V4 passes through the dura and foramen magnum to the ventral medulla. The vertebral arteries usually unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery. Medullary, spinal and PICA branches provide variable supply to the medulla, upper cord and inferior cerebellum.

afferent: Usually the proximal subclavian artery; vertebral origin variants occur
efferent: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery) — the largest branch, supplying the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum
Anterior spinal artery (the paired ventral branches that join in the midline) and small posterior spinal/paramedian medullary perforators
Basilar artery (vasc-basilar-artery) — formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction
Variable muscular, osseous and radicular branches arise along the cervical course; these are branches of the vertebral artery, with potential cervical anastomoses

bloodSupply: Inflow from the subclavian artery; distal branches include medullary perforators, anterior/posterior spinal branches and usually PICA.

clinical.findings: A lateral medullary infarct can produce ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain-temperature loss, ipsilateral ataxia and Horner syndrome, vertigo, nystagmus, dysphagia and hoarseness. The full constellation is not required, and vertebral or PICA disease can be responsible.
Paramedian injury can combine contralateral weakness and vibration-position loss with ipsilateral hypoglossal weakness. The triad is often incomplete.
clinical.vascular: Paramedian vertebral branches rostrally and anterior spinal branches more caudally

clinical.findings: May produce head/neck pain and posterior circulation ischaemia. Intracranial dissections can also rupture into the subarachnoid space.

name: Basilar artery
function: Single trunk formed by the vertebral arteries near the pontomedullary junction. It runs in the prepontine cistern along the ventral pons, gives paramedian and circumferential pontine branches, AICA and SCA, and usually divides into the PCAs. Different branches supply ventral pontine motor pathways and dorsal or lateral tegmental structures; the extent of injury from basilar disease depends on the occlusion site and collateral circulation.

afferent: Union of the two vertebral arteries (vasc-vertebral-artery) at the pontomedullary junction
Retrograde flow through the posterior communicating arteries from the anterior circulation — the collateral route that keeps a basilar occlusion survivable in some patients
efferent: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery) — the circumferential branch at the pontomedullary/pontine junction
Superior cerebellar artery (vasc-superior-cerebellar-artery) — the last named branch before the bifurcation
Paired posterior cerebral arteries (vasc-posterior-cerebral-artery) as the terminal bifurcation; numerous paramedian and short/long circumferential perforators to the pons

bloodSupply: Inflow from both vertebral arteries; branches supply the pons and contribute to cerebellar, midbrain and posterior cerebral circulation. Communicating-artery collateral flow is variable.

clinical.findings: Bilateral ventral pontine injury can cause quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved awareness; vertical eye movements and blinking are often retained in the classic form. Basilar occlusion can also cause impaired consciousness or other syndromes when the tegmentum is affected.

A unilateral dorsal pontine lesion of the PPRF or abducens nucleus plus the ipsilateral MLF causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy and internuclear ophthalmoplegia; the other eye can still abduct. Infarction is one possible cause.

Caudal pontine lesions can combine ipsilateral facial or abducens dysfunction with contralateral weakness; dorsal extension may add gaze palsy and sensory loss. Findings depend on the actual lesion rather than on an eponym alone.

Distal basilar disease can affect variable combinations of rostral midbrain, thalami, occipital and medial temporal regions, causing altered consciousness, eye movement abnormalities, memory impairment and visual deficits.

name: Anterior cerebral artery
synonyms: A1/A2/A3 segments of the anterior cerebral artery
function: ACA arises from the ICA and courses medially toward the anterior communicating artery. Distal branches curve around and above the corpus callosum to supply much of the medial frontal and anterior medial parietal cortex, including the paracentral leg/foot sensorimotor region, and portions of the corpus callosum. Deep ACA branches, including the recurrent artery of Heubner, supply parts of the anterior basal ganglia and internal capsule. Territory boundaries and branch patterns vary.

afferent: ICA A1 segment
ACoA collateral connection with the opposite ACA
efferent: Heubner artery near the ACA-ACoA junction or proximal A2, occasionally A1; other ACA perforators
Pericallosal, callosomarginal and variable medial frontal/parietal cortical branches

bloodSupply: Inflow usually from the ipsilateral ICA through A1; the ACoA can provide cross-flow from the opposite A1. A1 asymmetry and distal ACA variants alter this pattern.

clinical.findings: Usually causes contralateral leg-predominant weakness and sensory loss. Abulia, impaired initiation, grasp reflexes, incontinence, language disturbance or an alien hand can occur with medial frontal/callosal involvement. Large infarcts can affect the arm as well.

Injury may impair transfer of motor or language-related information between hemispheres, causing left-hand apraxia or agraphia in a typical left language-dominant brain; alien-hand phenomena can have frontal or callosal mechanisms.
clinical.vascular: ACA callosal and medial frontal branches

clinical.findings: Bilateral medial frontal infarction can cause severe abulia or akinetic mutism and bilateral leg weakness. An azygos/bihemispheric distal ACA or one dominant A1 feeding both sides can increase shared vulnerability, but variants are not equivalent.

name: Anterior communicating artery
function: Short connection between the two ACAs at the anterior circle of Willis. It can redistribute blood between the A1/A2 systems when pressure gradients permit, but a complete effective collateral route is not present in everyone. Small perforators supply parts of the anterior hypothalamic, septal/basal forebrain and optic-chiasm region. It is a common intracranial aneurysm site.

afferent: ACA A1 segments, with flow direction determined by pressure and individual anatomy
efferent: ACA A2 segments as a communicating collateral route
Small hypothalamic, septal and chiasmatic perforators

bloodSupply: Inflow through the ACA A1 segments. Its direct perforators supply a limited basal forebrain/hypothalamic region; cortical ACA territory is a potential collateral destination, not its direct tissue territory.

clinical.findings: Rupture can cause sudden severe headache, meningism and altered consciousness. Basal forebrain injury or damage to adjacent perforators may add memory or behavioural dysfunction; sufficiently large aneurysms may compress the optic apparatus.
Injury to hypothalamic or basal forebrain perforators, including during aneurysm treatment, can cause memory, behavioural or autonomic/endocrine dysfunction depending on the territory involved.

name: Middle cerebral artery
synonyms: M1/M2/M3/M4 segments of the middle cerebral artery
function: Major ICA terminal artery. M1 travels laterally toward the Sylvian fissure and gives deep lenticulostriate perforators; insular M2, opercular M3 and cortical M4 branches supply most of the lateral frontal, parietal and temporal cortex and underlying white matter. ACA and PCA territories border this distribution, so the entire lateral surface is not uniformly MCA territory. Superior/inferior division anatomy is variable.

afferent: Internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery) at its intracranial terminal bifurcation

Collateral flow through the circle of Willis (anterior communicating and posterior communicating arteries) and, in the acute setting, through leptomeningeal anastomoses from the ACA and PCA on the convexity
efferent: Lateral lenticulostriate perforators (vasc-lenticulostriate-arteries) from M1 — the deep supply to the putamen, caudate and internal capsule
Orbitofrontal and temporopolar branches, anterior temporal branches, insular (M2) branches, and the superior and inferior division trunks that fan out over the convexity

bloodSupply: Inflow from the ICA. Lenticulostriate branches supply parts of the basal ganglia and internal capsule; surface branches supply lateral cortex and subcortical white matter, with variable leptomeningeal collateral connections.

clinical.findings: Combined cortical and deep injury can produce contralateral hemiplegia, sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia and gaze preference toward the lesion, with global aphasia in a language-dominant hemisphere or neglect in the other hemisphere. Large infarcts may develop dangerous swelling.
clinical.vascular: MCA stem / combined divisions and perforators

clinical.findings: Often causes contralateral face/arm-predominant weakness and sometimes cortical sensory loss; dominant frontal involvement can cause nonfluent aphasia.

Can cause fluent aphasia in the dominant hemisphere or neglect in the other hemisphere, with a contralateral field deficit and relatively little weakness. The field pattern depends on involved cortex and white matter.
Capsular involvement can cause pure motor or sensorimotor deficits; a larger striatocapsular lesion may have more complex findings.

name: Posterior communicating artery
function: Connects the supraclinoid ICA to the PCA at the P1-P2 junction. Perforators supply variable hypothalamic, subthalamic, optic-tract and anterior thalamic regions; the tuberothalamic artery usually arises here. In a fetal PCA configuration, carotid inflow through a large PCoA is dominant and P1 is hypoplastic or absent. This changes occipital embolic supply, but not necessarily all thalamic perforator origins.

afferent: Supraclinoid ICA
Possible PCA-to-ICA collateral flow in an appropriate pressure gradient
efferent: PCA at the P1-P2 junction
Variable perforators, including the tuberothalamic/premammillary artery, to anterior thalamic and hypothalamic regions

bloodSupply: Usually receives ICA inflow; cross-flow between the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems depends on vessel calibre and pressure. Fetal PCA anatomy carries dominant ICA-to-PCA flow.

clinical.syndrome: ICA-PCoA aneurysm with CN III palsy
clinical.findings: An aneurysm can compress the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve, producing ptosis, diplopia, impaired adduction/elevation/depression and often pupillary dilation. Pupil sparing does not by itself exclude compression.
Can cause disorientation, memory disturbance, abulia and sometimes dominant-hemisphere language impairment; territory varies with anterior thalamic arterial anatomy.
Injury to motor basal ganglia circuitry can cause contralateral hemichorea/hemiballismus; the responsible lesion need not be confined to the STN.
Carotid embolism may cause PCA cortical infarction because the carotid is the dominant inflow to that PCA. This is an anatomical variant, not itself a disease.

name: Posterior cerebral artery
synonyms: P1/P2/P3/P4 segments of the posterior cerebral artery (precommunicating, ambient, quadrigeminal, cortical)
function: Usually the terminal basilar branch. P1 extends to the PCoA junction; P2 curves around the midbrain, and distal branches reach the medial/inferior temporal and occipital cortex. Separate perforator groups supply much of the thalamus and portions of the midbrain; posterior choroidal branches supply choroid plexus and adjacent tissue. Cortical and deep deficits depend on which branches are affected, and fetal PCA anatomy alters inflow.

afferent: Basilar artery (vasc-basilar-artery) at the basilar bifurcation (P1)
Posterior communicating artery (vasc-posterior-communicating-artery) at the P1–P2 junction — the anterior-posterior anastomosis, and the dominant inflow in the fetal-type configuration
efferent: Posterior thalamoperforating (paramedian) arteries, thalamogeniculate arteries and the posterior choroidal arteries (medial and lateral) to the thalamus and choroid plexus
Temporal branches (hippocampal, anterior and posterior temporal) to the medial temporal lobe, and the calcarine and parieto-occipital branches to the visual cortex
Midbrain perforators to the colliculi, pretectum, red nucleus, oculomotor nucleus and crus cerebri

bloodSupply: Usually basilar inflow through P1, with carotid communication through PCoA; ICA inflow dominates in a fetal PCA. Distal anastomoses may provide collateral flow.

clinical.findings: Often produces a contralateral homonymous field defect; macular sparing may occur but is not obligatory. Dominant occipital-splenial involvement can cause alexia without agraphia, and medial temporal involvement may affect memory.

A single P1-origin perforator variant supplies both paramedian thalami, sometimes with rostral midbrain. Occlusion can cause altered consciousness, memory dysfunction and vertical gaze abnormalities; this is one mechanism of bilateral thalamic injury.
Contralateral sensory loss may be followed by central post-stroke pain. Sensory deficits and pain vary and need not both occur.
May cause cortical visual impairment or blindness with preserved pupillary reflexes; medial temporal or association-cortex involvement can add memory or higher visual dysfunction.

name: Superior cerebellar artery
function: Usually arises from the distal basilar artery just before the PCA. It courses around the upper pons/caudal midbrain, normally below CN III, and supplies the superior cerebellar surface, superior vermis, much of the deep cerebellar white matter and nuclei, and parts of the superior cerebellar peduncle. Small brainstem branches have variable overlapping territory; the tectum/red nucleus are not assigned wholesale to the SCA.

afferent: Distal basilar artery, usually just proximal to the PCA origin
efferent: Superior cerebellar hemispheric and vermian branches
Branches to deep cerebellar tissue, SCP and a variable small rostral pontine/caudal midbrain region

bloodSupply: Inflow usually from the distal basilar artery; origin and cerebellar branch distribution vary and overlap neighbouring cerebellar arteries.

clinical.findings: Usually produces ipsilateral limb/gait ataxia, dysmetria and dysarthria; associated brainstem signs depend on proximal branch involvement.

A large infarct in any major cerebellar artery territory may obstruct the fourth ventricle or compress the brainstem, causing deterioration. The need for an intervention depends on clinical and imaging findings.

name: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
function: Usually arises from the lower basilar artery and courses toward the cerebellopontine angle. Supplies variable lateral caudal pontine territory, middle cerebellar peduncle, flocculus and anteroinferior cerebellum. The labyrinthine artery usually arises from AICA but may arise directly from the basilar artery. Relationships to CN VII/VIII and cerebellar territories vary.

afferent: Basilar artery (vasc-basilar-artery) at the pontomedullary/pontine junction level
efferent: Internal auditory (labyrinthine) artery to the cochlea and vestibular labyrinth — the branch whose occlusion causes the deafness of the syndrome
Cerebellar branches to the flocculus, the anteroinferior cerebellar hemisphere and the middle cerebellar peduncle
Pontine tegmental branches to the facial and vestibulocochlear nuclei, the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, and the middle cerebellar peduncle

bloodSupply: Inflow usually from the basilar artery. The AICA/PICA cerebellar border and labyrinthine branch origin vary.

clinical.findings: May combine ipsilateral facial weakness, hearing loss, vertigo, ataxia and facial pain-temperature loss with contralateral body pain-temperature loss. Individual findings depend on the involved branches, and the complete pattern is uncommon.
Can cause acute sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo, either in isolation or with pontine/cerebellar stroke. These symptoms have nonvascular causes as well.
An AICA or another vascular loop may contribute to facial or vestibular nerve compression syndromes. Mere contact on imaging does not establish symptomatic compression.

name: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
function: Usually arises from the vertebral artery. Its variable course wraps around the medulla and cerebellar tonsil to the inferior vermis and hemisphere. The commonly described five segments are anterior medullary, lateral medullary, tonsillomedullary, telovelotonsillar and cortical. Medullary perforators share lateral medullary supply with vertebral branches; distal branches also supply fourth-ventricular choroid plexus.

afferent: Usually vertebral artery, with variable PICA origin/course
efferent: Medullary perforators to variable lateral medullary territory
Distal inferior cerebellar, vermian and fourth-ventricular choroidal branches

bloodSupply: Inflow usually from the vertebral artery; origins, loops and balance with AICA/SCA vary.

clinical.findings: Can cause ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain-temperature loss, ataxia and Horner syndrome with vertigo, dysphagia and hoarseness. Strength is often preserved, but extensions and incomplete patterns occur. Vertebral disease is also an important cause.
Vertigo, nausea and gait/limb ataxia may occur. A large infarct can cause fourth-ventricular obstruction or brainstem compression as it swells.
A proximal or distal PICA aneurysm may rupture into the subarachnoid space, sometimes with intraventricular blood; associated deficits depend on haemorrhage and neighbouring tissue injury.

name: Lenticulostriate arteries
function: Umbrella term for striate perforators supplying parts of the basal ganglia and internal capsule. Lateral lenticulostriate branches usually arise from proximal MCA; medial striate branches arise from ACA, with the recurrent artery of Heubner usually near the ACA-ACoA junction or proximal A2. Deep perforator territories have limited collateralization and are vulnerable to small-vessel infarction or haemorrhage. The separate lateral and medial records provide group detail; the model does not encode a universal branch count.

afferent: MCA M1 for the lateral group
ACA branches, including variable-origin Heubner artery, for the medial group
efferent: Parts of caudate, putamen, pallidum and internal capsule; distribution overlaps anterior choroidal and other perforators

bloodSupply: Parent inflow is MCA for lateral branches and ACA for medial branches. Functional end-artery behaviour does not establish a complete absence of every microscopic anastomosis.

clinical.findings: A small capsular lesion may cause pure motor or sensorimotor deficits, ataxic hemiparesis or dysarthria-clumsy hand without typical cortical signs. Pure sensory stroke classically localizes to thalamic rather than lenticulostriate territory.
clinical.vascular: Striate / other deep perforators according to location

clinical.findings: Hypertension-related small-vessel injury can cause basal ganglia haemorrhage with contralateral weakness or sensory loss; large haemorrhages may extend into ventricles or cause mass effect.

name: Anterior choroidal artery
synonyms: anterior choroidal artery (cisternal and plexal segments)
function: Usually arises from the supraclinoid ICA distal to the PCoA and courses posteriorly near the optic tract before entering the choroidal fissure/temporal horn plexus. Supplies variable parts of the posterior internal capsule, optic tract/geniculocalcarine pathway, pallidum and medial temporal structures, and lateral-ventricular choroid plexus. Individual territory overlaps neighbouring perforators and choroidal arteries.

afferent: Internal carotid artery (vasc-internal-carotid-artery), supraclinoid segment, just above the posterior communicating artery
efferent: Cisternal branches to the optic tract, the uncus, the amygdala, the hippocampus and the globus pallidus
Plexal branches entering the temporal horn through the choroidal fissure to supply the choroid plexus of the temporal horn and atrium
Retrolenticular branches to the optic radiation and the posterior limb of the internal capsule — the fibres whose loss defines the capsular triad

bloodSupply: Inflow usually from the ICA. Cisternal branches supply deep neural tissue; plexal branches supply choroid plexus, not the CSF cavity itself.

clinical.findings: The classical combination is contralateral weakness, sensory loss and homonymous field loss; partial syndromes are common and depend on capsular and visual pathway involvement.

The artery can be at risk during aneurysm or medial temporal/intraventricular procedures. Occlusion can injure eloquent deep tissue; outcome is variable rather than invariably a complete dense hemiplegia.

name: Medial posterior choroidal artery
function: One or more PCA branches that curve around the midbrain toward the pineal/habenular region and tela choroidea of the third ventricle. Medial posterior choroidal branches supply third-ventricular choroid plexus and variable medial/posterior thalamic and epithalamic tissue. The distinct lateral posterior choroidal group enters the lateral-ventricular choroidal fissure and contributes to body/atrial plexus supply; it is not fully represented by this medial course.

afferent: PCA, with variable P1/P2 origin
efferent: Third-ventricular choroid plexus and variable medial thalamic/epithalamic branches
Anastomotic contributions to adjacent choroidal territory; the lateral posterior choroidal arteries are a distinct group

bloodSupply: Inflow from variable proximal PCA branches, commonly P1 or P2. Medial and lateral posterior choroidal territories are distinct but can overlap.

clinical.findings: Injury may affect thalamic/epithalamic tissue or choroid plexus depending on the branches involved. Exact sensory, visual or memory findings cannot be inferred from this single schematic course.
Choroidal arteries may feed intraventricular tumors; medial/lateral posterior and anterior choroidal contributions vary with tumor location.
